atomicity.title: A transfer that dies halfway
atomicity.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Session A starts a transfer and takes 100 from Ana, then the second update fails a check constraint. The transaction is aborted, and a rollback leaves both balances as they began. A third connection sees 500 and 100 at every step.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: The transaction opens. Nothing has changed yet.

steps.sql: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Ana's balance drops by 100 inside this transaction. A third connection still sees 500, because nothing is committed.

steps.sql: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 200 WHERE id = 2
steps.note: This update would take Ben below zero. The CHECK constraint rejects it, so the statement fails.
steps.error: new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "accounts_balance_check"

steps.sql: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Postgres won't run anything else now. After one failure the whole transaction is aborted, so the only useful command left is ROLLBACK.
steps.error: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Even COMMIT can't save it: Postgres answers ROLLBACK. Ana's 100 comes back and the row was never visibly changed. That's atomicity working.

dirty.title: Can a report see uncommitted work?
dirty.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL at read uncommitted. Session A changes a quantity without committing. Session B, asking for read uncommitted, still reads the old committed total, because PostgreSQL treats that level as read committed.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED
steps.note: Session B asks for the weakest level the SQL standard defines.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: The real total.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: Session A starts a change.

steps.sql: UPDATE sales SET quantity = 5 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Session A raises a quantity but hasn't committed. A dirty read would now show B a total that may never be real.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: B still gets the committed total. Postgres accepts READ UNCOMMITTED but runs it as READ COMMITTED, so a dirty read can't happen here at all.

steps.sql: ROLLBACK
steps.note: Session A changes its mind. Any reader that had seen its number would now be holding a value that never existed.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Done.

dirty-mysql.title: The same run on MySQL
dirty-mysql.alt: A recorded run on MySQL at read uncommitted. Session A changes a quantity without committing, session B's total rises to the uncommitted value, then session A rolls back and B's next total drops again. B saw a dirty read of a value that never existed.

steps.sql: SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED
steps.note: MySQL really implements this level.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: Session B opens a transaction.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: The real total.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: Session A starts a change.

steps.sql: UPDATE sales SET quantity = 5 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Session A raises a quantity but hasn't committed.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: Here is the dirty read: B's total includes a change nobody has committed.

steps.sql: ROLLBACK
steps.note: Session A rolls back. The number B just read never existed.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: B's total falls back. If B had printed the earlier figure on a report, the report would be wrong for good.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Done.

non-repeatable.title: Two reads inside one transaction
non-repeatable.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL with one tab per isolation level. Session B reads a total, session A commits a change, and B reads again. At read committed the second read differs from the first. At repeatable read and serializable it matches.

variants.label: Read committed
variants.summary: The report's two reads disagree: each statement got its own fresh snapshot.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED
steps.note: Session B starts a report at READ COMMITTED.

steps.sql: SELECT product, sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY product ORDER BY product
steps.note: The first read: revenue per product, which adds up to 330.

steps.sql: UPDATE sales SET quantity = quantity + 5 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Session A commits a change between B's two reads. Outside a transaction block, a statement commits at once.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: The second read, in the same transaction, for the report footer. Does it still add up to 330?

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: The report ends.

variants.label: Repeatable read
variants.summary: Both reads agree, because the whole transaction reads from one snapshot.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: Session B starts a report at REPEATABLE READ.

steps.sql: SELECT product, sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY product ORDER BY product
steps.note: The first read: revenue per product, which adds up to 330.

steps.sql: UPDATE sales SET quantity = quantity + 5 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Session A commits a change between B's two reads. Outside a transaction block, a statement commits at once.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: The second read, in the same transaction, for the report footer. Does it still add up to 330?

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: The report ends.

variants.label: Serializable
variants.summary: Both reads agree, because the whole transaction reads from one snapshot.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: Session B starts a report at SERIALIZABLE.

steps.sql: SELECT product, sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY product ORDER BY product
steps.note: The first read: revenue per product, which adds up to 330.

steps.sql: UPDATE sales SET quantity = quantity + 5 WHERE id = 1
steps.note: Session A commits a change between B's two reads. Outside a transaction block, a statement commits at once.

steps.sql: SELECT sum(quantity * price) AS revenue FROM sales
steps.note: The second read, in the same transaction, for the report footer. Does it still add up to 330?

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: The report ends.

phantom.title: A new row appears mid-report
phantom.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL with one tab per isolation level. Session B counts phone sales, session A inserts and commits a new one, and B counts again. At read committed the count rises from 2 to 3. At repeatable read and serializable it stays at 2.

variants.label: Read committed
variants.summary: The second count includes a row that didn't exist for the first: a phantom.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED
steps.note: Session B starts counting at READ COMMITTED.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Two phone sales.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO sales (product, quantity, price) VALUES ('Phone', 1, 100)
steps.note: Session A inserts a matching row and commits it. No existing row changed, so locks on the rows B read wouldn't have stopped this.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Session B counts again.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Done.

variants.label: Repeatable read
variants.summary: No phantom. The SQL standard allows one at repeatable read, but Postgres goes further because the level is a snapshot.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: Session B starts counting at REPEATABLE READ.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Two phone sales.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO sales (product, quantity, price) VALUES ('Phone', 1, 100)
steps.note: Session A inserts a matching row and commits it. No existing row changed, so locks on the rows B read wouldn't have stopped this.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Session B counts again.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Done.

variants.label: Serializable
variants.summary: No phantom. The SQL standard allows one at repeatable read, but Postgres goes further because the level is a snapshot.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: Session B starts counting at SERIALIZABLE.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Two phone sales.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO sales (product, quantity, price) VALUES ('Phone', 1, 100)
steps.note: Session A inserts a matching row and commits it. No existing row changed, so locks on the rows B read wouldn't have stopped this.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Session B counts again.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Done.

phantom-mysql.title: The phantom on MySQL
phantom-mysql.alt: A recorded run on MySQL at repeatable read. Session B counts two phone sales, session A inserts a third and commits. B's plain count stays at two, but a locking read in the same transaction sees three, because locking reads look at the latest committed rows.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: MySQL's default is REPEATABLE READ.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS phones FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Two phone sales, read from a snapshot.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO sales (product, quantity, price) VALUES ('Phone', 1, 100)
steps.note: Session A inserts and commits a third.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS phones FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: A plain read still says two: it uses the same snapshot, so there's no phantom.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS phones FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone' FOR SHARE
steps.note: A locking read isn't a snapshot read. It looks at the latest committed rows, and the third phone appears inside the same transaction.

steps.sql: UPDATE sales SET price = 90 WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: An UPDATE works on the latest rows too. It reports three rows changed, one of which this transaction's snapshot says doesn't exist.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS phones FROM sales WHERE product = 'Phone'
steps.note: Now the plain read says three: a transaction always sees its own changes, so the updated phantom joins the snapshot.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Done. This is the behaviour behind the claim that MySQL's repeatable read isn't the same as Postgres's.

lost-update.title: Two people update the same stock count
lost-update.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL with tabs for read committed and repeatable read. Both sessions read 10 phones in stock and each wants to sell some. At read committed the second write waits, then overwrites, and one sale is lost. At repeatable read the second write fails with a serialization error and has to retry.

variants.label: Read committed
variants.summary: Two sales of 3 and 2 should leave 5 units. The table says 8, so session A's sale vanished without an error. That's a lost update.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED
steps.note: Session A starts a sale of 3.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED
steps.note: Session B starts a sale of 2.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A reads 10 and works out 10 - 3 = 7 in the application.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B reads 10 too and works out 10 - 2 = 8.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 7 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A writes the value it computed. It now holds the row lock.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 8 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B wants the same row and has to wait for A to finish.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: A commits, which releases the lock, and B's statement returns.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: B commits whatever state it's in.

variants.label: Repeatable read
variants.summary: Session B can't overwrite a row that changed after its snapshot. It gets an error, retries from a fresh read, and the count comes out right.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: Session A starts a sale of 3.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: Session B starts a sale of 2.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A reads 10 and works out 10 - 3 = 7 in the application.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B reads 10 too and works out 10 - 2 = 8.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 7 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A writes the value it computed. It now holds the row lock.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 8 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B wants the same row and has to wait for A to finish.

resolved.error: could not serialize access due to concurrent update

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: A commits, which releases the lock, and B's statement returns.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: B commits whatever state it's in.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: The application retries the whole transaction, as the error asks it to.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: This time B reads 7 and works out 7 - 2 = 5.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 5 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: No conflict now.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Both sales counted.

variants.label: Read committed, relative update
variants.summary: No error and no lost sale, at the weakest level. Letting the database do the arithmetic means the waiting UPDATE recomputes from the row A committed.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: Session A starts a sale of 3.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: Session B starts a sale of 2.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = units - 3 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A lets the database do the arithmetic, instead of writing a value it computed.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = units - 2 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B waits for A's row lock.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: A commits. Postgres re-reads the row for B's waiting UPDATE and subtracts from 7, not from 10.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: 5 units left, the right answer.

write-skew.title: Two doctors go off call at once
write-skew.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL with tabs for repeatable read and serializable. Two doctors are on call and the rule says at least one must stay. Each session sees two on call and takes its own doctor off. At repeatable read both commit and nobody is on call. At serializable the second commit fails with a serialization error.

variants.label: Repeatable read
variants.summary: Both transactions committed and nobody is on call. They touched different rows, so no row conflict was ever visible.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: Adam wants to go off call, at REPEATABLE READ.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ
steps.note: So does Bob.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: The rule is that at least one doctor stays on call. Adam sees two, so leaving looks safe.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: Bob sees two as well.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Adam'
steps.note: Adam updates his own row.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Bob'
steps.note: Bob updates his own row. It's a different row, so there's no lock to wait for.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Adam commits.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Bob commits, if the database lets him.

variants.label: Serializable
variants.summary: Postgres saw that the two transactions couldn't have run in any serial order and failed one. Nothing blocked: the loser retried, saw one doctor left and stayed on call.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: Adam wants to go off call, at SERIALIZABLE.

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: So does Bob.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: The rule is that at least one doctor stays on call. Adam sees two, so leaving looks safe.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: Bob sees two as well.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Adam'
steps.note: Adam updates his own row.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Bob'
steps.note: Bob updates his own row. It's a different row, so there's no lock to wait for.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Adam commits.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: Bob commits, if the database lets him.
steps.error: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions

steps.sql: BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: The application retries Bob's transaction.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: Now Bob sees one doctor on call, himself, so he can't leave.

steps.sql: ROLLBACK
steps.note: Bob stays on call and the rule holds.

write-skew-lock.title: The same doctors with a lock
write-skew-lock.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL at read committed. Each doctor's session locks the on-call rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE. Bob's lock waits for Adam to commit, then sees only one doctor on call, so Bob stays. No error and no retry, but Bob had to wait.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: This time at plain READ COMMITTED.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: Same for Bob.

steps.sql: SELECT name FROM doctors WHERE on_call FOR UPDATE
steps.note: Adam locks every row he based the decision on, not only his own.

steps.sql: SELECT name FROM doctors WHERE on_call FOR UPDATE
steps.note: Bob asks for the same locks and waits.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Adam'
steps.note: Two were on call, so Adam leaves.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: The locks are released and Bob's query returns. It rechecks the rows, so it lists only Bob.

steps.sql: ROLLBACK
steps.note: Bob sees one doctor left and stays. The rule holds, with no error to handle.

rr-mysql.title: Lost update at MySQL's repeatable read
rr-mysql.alt: A recorded run on MySQL at repeatable read. Both sessions read 10 units and write values computed in the application. The second write waits for the first, then succeeds and overwrites, so MySQL's default level allows the lost update that PostgreSQL's level rejects.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: Both sessions run at MySQL's default, REPEATABLE READ.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: Session B begins.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A reads 10.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B reads 10.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 7 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: A writes its result.

steps.sql: UPDATE stock SET units = 8 WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: B waits for A's row lock.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: A commits. B's update returns successfully, with no error.

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: B commits.

steps.sql: SELECT units FROM stock WHERE item = 'Phone'
steps.note: 8 units. A's sale is lost at the same level name that protected it on Postgres.

write-skew-mysql.title: Serializable on MySQL is built from locks
write-skew-mysql.alt: A recorded run on MySQL at serializable. Each doctor's read takes a shared lock. Adam's update then has to wait for Bob's shared lock, and Bob's update waits for Adam's, which is a deadlock. MySQL rolls Bob back with a deadlock error, Adam's update goes through, and the rule holds.

steps.sql: SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: Adam's connection asks for MySQL's strictest level.

steps.sql: SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE
steps.note: Bob's too.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: Adam begins.

steps.sql: START TRANSACTION
steps.note: Bob begins.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: At this level InnoDB turns a plain SELECT into a locking read, so Adam now holds shared locks on the rows.

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) AS on_call FROM doctors WHERE on_call
steps.note: Shared locks don't conflict, so Bob reads and holds them too.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Adam'
steps.note: Adam needs an exclusive lock on his row, and Bob's shared lock is in the way, so he waits. This is the blocking my notes described.

steps.sql: UPDATE doctors SET on_call = false WHERE name = 'Bob'
steps.note: Now Bob needs a row Adam has locked. Each waits for the other: a deadlock. MySQL picks a victim straight away.
steps.error: Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

steps.sql: COMMIT
steps.note: The survivor commits.

steps.sql: SELECT name, on_call FROM doctors ORDER BY name
steps.note: One doctor stays on call. The rule held, and the price was a wait and an error instead of a clean retry signal.

exit.title: Walking away from an open transaction
exit.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Session one begins a transaction, takes 10 phones out of inventory and sees 90, then disconnects without committing. A new connection reads the inventory and finds 100, because the unfinished transaction was rolled back.

steps.sql: BEGIN
steps.note: The transaction starts.

steps.sql: UPDATE products SET inventory = inventory - 10
steps.note: Ten phones leave the inventory.

steps.sql: SELECT name, inventory FROM products
steps.note: Inside the transaction the change is real: 90.

steps.sql: \q
steps.note: The client quits without COMMIT. To the server, an open transaction on a closed connection is an abandoned one.

steps.sql: SELECT name, inventory FROM products
steps.note: A new connection finds 100. The unfinished work is gone, which is atomicity doing its job.

transfer.title: Commit and rollback
transfer.hint: Run the transfer, then try the presets. Each run starts from whatever the last one left, and Reset puts the balances back.
transfer.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text, balance int NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Ana', 500), (2, 'Ben', 100);

presets.label: Change your mind
See the transaction id

rule-break.title: Ask the database to break its own rule
rule-break.hint: The CHECK constraint is a consistency rule you defined. This run fails on purpose: read the error, then add a smaller amount.
rule-break.setup:
CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text, balance int NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Ana', 500), (2, 'Ben', 100);
rule-break.query: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 700 WHERE id = 1;

presets.label: What's in the table now?
presets.sql: SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

presets.label: A foreign key rule
presets.sql:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payments (account_id int REFERENCES accounts(id), amount int);
INSERT INTO payments VALUES (99, 10);
